newsitem.title: USA: Environment, jobs, Russia featured at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Environment, jobs, Russia featured at G7 summit.

text.p: For once, the annual summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations plus Russia was not hijacked by an economic or political crisis.
"This is not a moment of high drama," President Clinton's spokesman, Mike McCurry, said.
The result was that world leaders had the luxury of examining questions such as the lack of economic security and aging populations that are of growing concern to their peoples.
"These are the issues that now dominate a global summit like this, and that is a very very positive thing," he said.
Following are some of the more contentious issues tackled in Denver.

ENVIRONMENT -- The European Union failed in its attempts to persuade the United States, backed by Canada and Japan, to agree to specific targets for reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and other so-called greenhouse gases that cause global warming.

The G7 urged significant cuts in emissions, but the EU, led by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, had hoped for clear-cut targets ahead of Monday's earth summit at the United Nations in New York. Kohl said the summit was "split into two blocs".

JOBS -- Much of the economic debate at the summit was about how the rest of the G7 could learn about flexible labour markets from the United States, whose low employment rate is the envy of the world.

Britain eagerly embraced the U.S. lead and vowed to put employability at the top of next year's G7 summit in Birmingham, England. But France put up stubborn resistance, with President Jacques Chirac firmly ruling out importing the U.S. model: "We have our own traditions, our own model, and we want to keep it."

RUSSIA - Apart from a bout of tiredness that made him miss a late-night concert, President Boris Yeltsin can look back with pleasure at Denver as the summit at which Russia was almost accepted as a fully paid-up member of the world's movers and shakers.

He attended all this year's plenaries, except for a one-hour session on economics and finance, and Russia was accepted as a member of the influential Paris Club of creditor governments. Yeltsin said he also expected Russia to be a member of the World Trade Organisation by the end of 1997.

But Japan, which disputes with Moscow sovereignty over four Pacific islands, insisted Russia was "not ready" to join in discussions on macroeconomics and France said there was "no consensus" for full Russian membership.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair said this year's formula of including Russia in all but one session on financial matters worked well. He is likely to retain it at the 1998 summit.

HONG KONG - Eight days before Hong Kong reverts to China after more than 150 years as a British colony, the summit said it expected Beijing to honour the commitments it made to protect Hong Kong's civil liberties and independent economic system after the handover.
Major issues addressed on the margins of the summit included:
BOSNIA - The leaders papered over differences over the time frame for the international peacekeeping force in Bosnia.

The United States says it will withdraw its 8,500 troops from the 31,000-strong force in June next year but European leaders say if American troops pull out they would also withdraw and the factional violence could resume.

The compromise in Denver was to put the emphasis not on the pull-out date but on urgent measures to build democratic and social systems to cement the peace. A statement said there would be financial penalties for groups which did not fully cooperate to implement the 1995 Dayton peace accords.

NATO - There was open dissent from some European NATO members against Clinton's determination that only three new members -- Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic -- be invited to join the western alliance in the first round of post-Cold War expansion.

France's President Chirac called for Romania to be included and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi backed both Romania and Slovenia. Prodi said he told Clinton he was making a "big mistake" adding: "There is a complete difference of opinion on this matter."

Germany, which originally supported Romania's membership, has taken an equivocal stand since Clinton announced his wish-list, saying the matter must be discussed. Britain backs the three states suppoorted by Clinton.
